name: Timecard
tagline: A small Mac app for clocking hours against projects and seeing where the day went.

pricing.notes: AI-drafted from a site submission; price unverified. Indie Mac apps like this are usually a one-time purchase, but that is an assumption, not a checked fact.

verdictSummary: A personal time tracker is close to the canonical one-shot build: a timer, a list of projects, a local database, and a weekly total. There is no network, no shared data, and nothing an agent cannot write in an afternoon with SwiftUI and SQLite. The part that is actually hard is the part nobody notices until it bites: surviving sleep and wake, not losing a running timer on crash, and being pleasant enough in the menu bar that you keep using it. Paid versions earn their money on polish and on the exports your accountant will accept, not on anything structural. If you bill hours for a living, the ten dollars is cheaper than debugging your own timer; if you just want to know where Tuesday went, build it.
coreLoopDIY: A macOS menu bar app with a start/stop timer bound to a project, local SQLite storage, a day and week summary, and CSV export.
requirements: Basic comfort running an Xcode build and granting an app login-item permission
Willingness to self-sign rather than pay for a developer certificate
whatYouLose: Automatic idle detection and the 'you left the timer running overnight' rescue prompt
Polished reporting: billable rates, rounding rules, invoice-ready PDFs
Sync across devices, and any iPhone companion for tracking away from the desk
Calendar or project-tool integrations that pre-fill what you were doing
A signed, notarized, auto-updating binary that just works after an OS upgrade
moatNotes: The moat is ergonomics. Time tracking fails from friction, not from missing features, and friction is exactly what indie Mac devs spend years sanding down.
whyPeopleStillPay: Because a time tracker you resent is a time tracker you stop using, and the difference between a tool you open daily and one you abandon in week two is a hundred small interactions: how fast the menu bar popover appears, whether it remembers your last project, whether it notices you went to lunch. A one-shot build gets you the data model and the timer, which is most of the code and almost none of the habit. For anyone invoicing clients there is also the boring stuff: rounding, rates, and an export that does not need manual cleanup before it goes anywhere near a bill.
notes: The timer is trivial; the discipline is not, and no app ships that.
prompt:
Build a macOS menu bar time tracking app called Clocky. Native, local only, no accounts.

Stack: Swift 5.9+, SwiftUI, MenuBarExtra for the menu bar UI, SQLite via GRDB for storage. Xcode project, macOS 14+ target. No server, no network calls, no analytics, no login.

Data model (SQLite file in Application Support/Clocky/clocky.sqlite):
- project: id, name, color hex, archived bool
- entry: id, project_id, started_at, ended_at nullable, note text

Features, in scope:
1. MenuBarExtra showing either the elapsed time of the running entry (format H:MM) or a small clock glyph when idle.
2. Popover with: a project picker, a big Start/Stop button, an optional one-line note field, and today's entries as a list with per-entry duration and an inline delete.
3. Exactly one entry can run at a time. Starting a new one stops the current one.
4. A Projects sheet to add, rename, assign a color, and archive projects. Seed with one project named General.
5. A Reports window: pick a date range (Today, This Week, Last 7 Days, This Month, Custom), show total hours plus a per-project breakdown with a simple bar for each project.
6. CSV export of the selected range: project,note,started_at,ended_at,duration_minutes. Save via NSSavePanel.
7. Idle guard: if the Mac sleeps or the display locks for more than 15 minutes with a timer running, on wake show a prompt offering to trim the entry back to the sleep timestamp or keep it. Use NSWorkspace sleep/wake notifications.
8. Crash safety: write started_at to the DB immediately on start, never hold a running entry only in memory. On launch, if an entry has a null ended_at, resume it as the running timer.
9. Global hotkey Cmd+Shift+T to toggle start/stop on the last used project.
10. Launch at login toggle using SMAppService.

Out of scope, do not build: iCloud or any sync, iOS app, hourly rates, invoicing, calendar integration, auto-detection of apps or websites, multi-user anything, updates framework.

Deliverables: the Xcode project, and a README with build instructions, where the database lives, and how to back it up by copying that one file. Write unit tests for duration math across day boundaries and for the sleep-trim logic.
